Then they saw their spiritual leader appear to abandon the cause when Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya made peace with the Umayyad ruler ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān.
The hope that had existed in the hidden depths of their still-unclear social awareness was shaken by these two blows. It began to collapse.
But their social awareness resisted complete defeat.
Instead, it turned toward a spiritual and supernatural escape from the unbearable feeling of hopelessness.

The belief that Ibn al-Ḥanafiyya would return was that escape. He had sinned, they believed, by making peace with the oppressive Umayyads, and God had temporarily hidden him away as punishment. But he would return.
For the Kaysāni mawālī of Kufa, this belief became a source of comfort.

Did it not offer some relief from Umayyad oppression, and from the contempt shown to them by Kufa’s Arab merchants, landowners, and rulers, who controlled their livelihoods, their bodies, and their human dignity?
And what greater comfort could there be than the promise that God would one day:
“raise up the knowing imam, Muḥammad, known as Abū al-Qāsim, in spite of all who oppose him and in spite of hostile time itself. He will rule the whole earth and wrench it from every defender”?
The second striking feature of the Kaysāni movement is pointed out by al-Ṭabarī. He writes:
“Every extremist among the Shiʿa used to gather with Hind bint al-Mutakallifa al-Nāʿiṭiyya, and they would hold discussions in her house and in the house of Laylā bint Qumāma al-Muzaniyya.”
Al-Ṭabarī is referring here to this same extremist Shiʿi group, the Kaysāniyya.

Both women were known historically to have been influenced by Kaysāni beliefs. They in turn influenced some of the women of Kufa, as well as a number of men who became active advocates of the movement.
One of these was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Nawf. Al-Ṭabarī himself tells us that Ibn Nawf left the house of Hind al-Nāʿiṭiyya when he went out to fight Muṣʿab ibn al-Zubayr.
Al-Jāḥiẓ described both women as devoted worshippers and ascetics.
It seems to us that the attraction of women in Kufa to the Kaysāni cause began, at first, as an emotional response to the killing of al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī and his family at Karbala.

Not long afterward, however, the movement to avenge al-Ḥusayn became linked with the movement of the Kaysāni mawālī. At that point, this emotional response developed into a religious belief centered on Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya, the son of ʿAlī and brother of al-Ḥusayn, the martyr of Karbala.
This, in broad outline, is the picture of the Kaysāniyya as the first Shiʿi group to become known for extremism.

Before discussing them, we gave a broad picture of the more moderate Shiʿa, who stood closer to the original foundations of Shiʿism. Most of the other Shiʿi sects appeared later than the period we are examining here.
6 - The Question of Knowledge Among the Shiʿa

What we have discussed so far about the Shiʿi theory of the imamate, both in its moderate and extremist forms, should make it fairly easy to understand how the different Shiʿi groups approached the question of knowledge.

The Imami Shiʿa, and especially the Twelvers, held that the imamate was a divine right and that the imam’s authority came from God, not from the community. They also believed that the imam was protected from error and that he had to be the most knowledgeable person of his age.

Knowledge of God, of the mysteries of the universe, creation, and the soul, and of the religious law that represents God’s law for humanity, comes first from the Prophet during his lifetime and then from the imam after the Prophet.

In every age, the imam is the authority through whom this knowledge is understood. There is no other authority equal to him, because the imam reports from the Prophet, and the Prophet reports from divine revelation.

Reason does have a role here, but only within strict limits. It may uncover arguments that support divine truths or prove them, but it cannot oppose those truths. Reason is unable by itself to reach the same level of knowledge about the truths of the universe and the mysteries of existence, much less the metaphysical mysteries of the universe and existence.
Here, as we saw in the first part of this study, knowledge remains tied to religious faith. It follows faith and is subject to what faith provides. Reason can operate only within those limits.

The moderate Shiʿa did accept ijtihād—independent reasoning—in matters of Islamic law. They never closed the door of ijtihād at any point in their history and continue to practice it today. This differs from the four main Sunni legal schools, which, according to this view, closed the door of ijtihād around the fourth Islamic century, or the tenth century CE.
But the continuing Shiʿi use of ijtihād does not change the basic religious character of their theory of knowledge.

This is because ijtihād is allowed only where there is no clear text in the Qurʾān, no clear statement from the Prophet, no clear statement from one of the Twelve Imams, and no established consensus among Shiʿi scholars.

When such a consensus exists, it means that the opinion of the infallible twelfth imam, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan—the hidden and awaited imam—is understood to be present somewhere within the opinions that make up that consensus.
Only when there is no evidence from the Qurʾān, from the transmitted sayings, or from consensus does the fourth source come into play: reason.
This fourth source rests on basic rational assumptions accepted by common social reason—what is known as general custom.
Muslim jurists organized these principles into a systematic body of thought, creating a distinct field known as uṣūl al-fiqh, the principles of Islamic jurisprudence.

This field is not limited to the Shiʿa. Sunni jurists also use it, though with some differences. One important difference is that what the Shiʿa call the evidence of reason corresponds, among Sunnis, to the use of analogy.
There is no doubt that uṣūl al-fiqh played a distinctive rational role in the development of knowledge, at least because it relied on basic principles of common social reason.

Through this rational approach, it organized Islamic law according to rules and principles with some of the features of a science. It also allowed Islamic law to take part in the wider process of development affecting all areas of social life during the great historical period of Arab-Islamic civilization.

Uṣūl al-fiqh also differed from the formal structure of Aristotelian logic. Its conclusions began from living, particular cases rather than from abstract or hypothetical operations carried out purely in the mind.
But the underlying theory of knowledge still restricted religious and legal knowledge to a divine source. This greatly narrowed the room available to reason, even in legal matters.
As a result, ijtihād remained very limited. Jurists developed a deep caution toward using reason to change or renew the law as life itself changed.
The Muʿtazilites made a bold attempt to give reason greater freedom in this area.

They accepted, for example, a principle known as rational istiṣḥāb, or the rational presumption of continuity. This meant that reason could make an independent judgment about certain matters, and that this judgment could remain in force over time until transmitted evidence arrived—meaning a text received from a divine source—that overruled it.
Schools opposed to the Muʿtazila rejected this approach.
For example, after explaining the Muʿtazilite principle of rational istiṣḥāb, the judge Abū al-Ṭayyib writes:
“There is no disagreement among the Sunnis that one may not act on this basis, because reason has no authority in matters of revealed law.”
What we are saying here about uṣūl al-fiqh applies equally to Sunnis and Shiʿa.

Even though this field had a rational foundation, the rational principles it used to derive legal rulings remained within the limits of the most basic assumptions of common social reason. They did not rise to the level of more developed rational principles that function as concepts in the philosophical sense and give reason room for a greater degree of independence and creativity.
In the later age of kalām, the study of uṣūl al-fiqh became intertwined with theology. This may be what led Muṣṭafā ʿAbd al-Rāziq to include uṣūl al-fiqh within what he called “Islamic philosophy.”

He says that the subjects discussed in uṣūl al-fiqh are, for the most part, similar to the subjects discussed in the study of the foundations of religious belief—that is, kalām. Books on uṣūl al-fiqh even sometimes refer to certain topics as “theological principles” because they belong to the field of kalām.

But this similarity is not enough, by itself, to justify placing uṣūl al-fiqh within “Islamic philosophy,” unless we expand the meaning and subject matter of philosophy until it becomes as broad as it was among the ancients, when philosophy was considered the “science of the sciences.”
The overlap pointed out by ʿAbd al-Rāziq was not unique to uṣūl al-fiqh. It was a general feature of Arab-Islamic scholarship during the period when kalām and logic flourished.
Even Arabic grammar absorbed elements of kalām and logic. We can see this in the way grammarians tried to give theoretical reasons for many grammatical rules.

Yet grammar does not really require this kind of reasoning. Its rules are, after all, records and organized descriptions based on observing the language of poetry, its styles and structures, and the way Arabic words change according to meaning and the purpose of an expression.
Would it therefore make sense to classify grammar as philosophy simply because earlier grammarians sometimes used arguments borrowed from kalām when explaining its rules?
None of this means that we deny the highly rational method found in uṣūl al-fiqh. We have already emphasized that quality.
But the field remains within the limits of its own legal logic, which is tied to the concepts of Islamic law and to their connection with a divine source of knowledge.

At the same time, we should recognize something positive in the close interaction between the different branches of Arab culture at the time and the rational investigations of kalām. This interaction reflected one of the distinctive features of Arab thought: its tendency to treat different areas of thought as parts of a whole, rather than sharply separating speculative thinking from thinking based more directly on experience and practice.
C - The Kharijites: No Faith Without Action
As we mentioned earlier, the Kharijites emerged from the conflict between ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Muʿāwiya after the killing of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān.

The conflict became an armed struggle at the Battle of Ṣiffīn. The fighting ended with the famous arbitration episode. One of the two arbitrators, Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, deposed the man he represented, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, while the second arbitrator, ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, confirmed Muʿāwiya as caliph.
Al-Shahrastānī summarizes what happened as follows:

“The Kharijites first forced ʿAlī to accept arbitration. He had wanted to send ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās, but the Kharijites rejected this and said: ‘He is one of your own.’ They forced him instead to send Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī, on the condition that he judge according to the Book of God.
“But the outcome did not go as they had wanted. When ʿAlī then rejected the result, the Kharijites rebelled against him and said: ‘Why did you allow men to judge? Judgment belongs to God alone.’”
This is how al-Shahrastānī explains both the rise of the Kharijites and the origin of their name. As he puts it:
“Anyone who rebels against the rightful imam whom the community has agreed upon is called a Kharijite.”
The first slogan raised by the Kharijites after the arbitration was:
“Judgment belongs to God, not to men.”
This was the first principle on which the rest of their theory was built.
“Right belongs to God.” No human being therefore has the right to dispose of it as he wishes, or to appoint another man to judge it according to personal desire.
This was the foundation of Kharijite thought.
From the moment they broke away from ʿAlī’s army at Ṣiffīn, they built their theoretical and practical positions toward every Islamic group and doctrine on this same principle.
Under this slogan, they went to Nahrawān and fought ʿAlī with the sword.

Applying the same principle, they argued that once a prophet had established a rule for his community, he could not turn back from it. Since ʿAlī had accepted arbitration over a right established by the Prophet, they argued that he had turned back from that right.
ʿAlī debated them on this point, but they refused to accept his argument.
They declared ʿAlī, ʿUthmān, and Muʿāwiya unbelievers. They did the same to everyone who had taken part in the Battle of the Camel and everyone who had accepted arbitration at Ṣiffīn.
They also publicly repented for their own sin in having accepted arbitration and raised the slogan of fighting all unbelievers.
Even after their defeat by ʿAlī’s army at Nahrawān, they did not abandon armed struggle.
They went so far as to assign two men from among themselves to carry out assassinations: one was to kill ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, and the other Muʿāwiya.
The first, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muljam, succeeded. The second failed.
After the death of ʿAlī, the Kharijites turned their struggle against the Umayyads.
On what basis did the Kharijites declare ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya unbelievers and say that they had to be fought?
Here we come to the second main element of their theory: their understanding of faith.
Their definition of faith differed from that of other Muslims.
From the time of the Prophet until then, faith had meant first an inward belief and then an outward declaration of that belief in words.
The Kharijites added a third element: outward action.
For them, it was not enough for someone to hold a belief inwardly. Belief and action had to match.
